BLOCK1.html: I’m Reaz Romen. I work at the seams between systems.

BLOCK2.html: I’m a systems engineer who works across embedded devices, networks, real-time communications, backend services and infrastructure. I’m most useful when a product crosses several of those layers and the problem does not belong cleanly to one team or one tool.

BLOCK3.html: A lot of my work is hands-on: ESP32-S3 firmware and audio, SIP/RTP call paths, Linux and Docker systems, observability, ingress, service control and the glue between them. The same pattern keeps showing up — the symptom appears in one layer while the root cause lives somewhere else.

BLOCK4.html: I prefer evidence over guesswork. I use serial logs, packet captures, timing measurements, metrics, controlled A/B builds and known-good baselines. I preserve working states before changing them, and I document the path so the system can be understood again later.

BLOCK5.html: Connected firmware, real-time voice paths, Linux infrastructure and operational tooling.

BLOCK6.html: Known-good baselines, logs, packets, timing, metrics, controlled changes and repeatable tests.

BLOCK7.html: Problems that cross device, network, media, service and infrastructure boundaries.

BLOCK8.html: I do not fit neatly into one engineering box.

BLOCK9.html: That is intentional. A connected product rarely fails according to an org chart. Firmware timing can surface as audio quality. SIP can succeed while RTP fails. A container can be “up” while the service is unusable. I like following the actual data path until the failure makes sense.

BLOCK10.html: Embedded: ESP32-S3, ESP-IDF/ADF, audio codecs, I2S/I2C, provisioning, OTA, controls and board bring-up.

BLOCK11.html: Voice: SIP, SDP, RTP, Asterisk, FreeSWITCH, OpenSIPS, Drachtio, endpoint and media-path debugging.

BLOCK12.html: Systems: Linux, Docker, ingress, observability, service health, logging, dependencies and recovery.

BLOCK14.html: Map boundaries, clocks, dependencies, data paths and the exact failure before changing behavior.

BLOCK16.html: Collect the evidence the system already has: logs, packets, timing, state, metrics and hardware behavior.

BLOCK18.html: Preserve a known-good control and change one part of the path at a time.

BLOCK20.html: Turn the hypothesis into the smallest useful change, then repeat the same failure test.

BLOCK22.html: Document architecture, verification and recovery so the system is easier to operate after the fix.

BLOCK24.html: Firmware for connected products where the device, hardware interfaces, network behavior and lifecycle all have to agree.

BLOCK26.html: SIP/RTP systems from endpoint behavior through PBX and media paths, including the failures that only appear during real calls.

BLOCK28.html: Linux and container infrastructure with clear ingress, health, observability, service state and recovery paths.

BLOCK30.html: For problems that refuse to stay in one box: audio that is really timing, calls that connect without media, or healthy processes behind broken services.

BLOCK31.html: A FEW THINGS I CARE ABOUT

BLOCK32.html: 01 Preserve a working state before “improving” it.

BLOCK33.html: 02 Make the system observable before tuning it.

BLOCK35.html: 04 Reproduce the same failure after the fix.

BLOCK36.html: 05 Leave documentation that survives the person who wrote it.

BLOCK38.html: If you want to understand the kind of problems that means in practice, the case studies are the best place to start.
